the presence of symptoms is predictive of consultation behaviour in both sexes but the presence of psychosocioal problems and distress is predictive of more frequent consultations only in women.
women are more likely than men to seek medical care for minor illness and this is related to the presence of psychosomatic symptoms and the presence of confidants.
the presence of psychosomatic problems and distress, the presence of confidants and contact with social agencies are associated with more frequent consultation in women.

the role of physical and psychosocial factors in explaining sex differences.
the social and psychological factors associated with attendance and help seeking behaviour in women and men.
the relationship between physical illness, psychosocial factors and help seeking behaviour.

women attend more frequently because they experience more physical illness.
women attend general practitioners more often than men because they are more physically ill and because their physical illnesses are more likely to be associated with psychosocial problems.

the sex differences in consultation rates are due to a combination of factors including the presence of illness and symptoms, the ability to disclose problems and the availability of social support networks.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the women were more likely to attend for help with physical symptoms and psychosocial problems and were more likely than the men to seek help for both types of problems.
women attend more frequently than men for physical symptoms and psychosocial problems.
the differences in attendance between the men and women were due to differences in the way the men and women responded to illness.
The main takeaway from our work is that
women's help seeking behaviour is more complex and multifaceted than men's, and that the presence of psychosomatic problems is a significant factor.
women attend more often for minor illness than men and that this difference is not explained by the presence of enabling factors or by the presence of physical illness.

the sex differences in attendance rates for minor illness in primary care are largely explained by the presence of physical illness in men and the presence of psychosomatic illness and distress in women.
